processing: An unoxidised green tea made from top-grade tender material and shaped flat and straight, resembling a bird's tongue, which is what queshe means.
harvest_season: Spring; as with other que she style greens, the earliest tender picking is the most prized.
appearance_dry: Flat, even, straight leaves in a vivid green with a little down.
taste_profile: A fresh, young-leaf aroma that lasts, then a brisk and clean cup with a returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Keep the water cool enough to protect the fresh aroma. A glass lets you watch the small leaves stand and settle.

vintage_note: Usually sold from the current spring's harvest and best within a year, as is normal for Sichuan greens. Grade and picking date matter more than any brand tier, so ask for both.
description:
Bashan Queshe is a flat green tea from Wanyuan in the Daba Mountains, in north-east Sichuan, associated particularly with Caoba town. Queshe means sparrow's tongue, a name used for small bud teas in several parts of China, so the Bashan is the part to look for.

The leaf is shaped flat and straight from tender material. The area is known for selenium-rich tea, a selling point you will see on packets, though the cup is what you should judge.

The local shorthand praises its green colour, high aroma, returning sweetness and neat shape. In practice that means a fresh young-leaf scent and a brisk, clean cup with sweetness arriving after the swallow. Cooler water keeps it that way; boiling water quickly turns it sharp.

The name is also tied to a company and a trademark, Sichuan's Bashan Queshe tea business, so you will see it sold as a brand as well as a regional style. Check for Wanyuan as the origin and for the harvest date.
history:
The tea in its present form is modern. One English-language tea reference, the only source found for these dates, says Wanyuan specialists developed the method in 1985, the state-run Caoba tea farm began industrial production in 1987, and the trademark was registered in 1989; a travel account instead puts the adoption of the name in 1984, so treat the chronology as approximate.

Claims about far older tea cultivation in this part of Sichuan concern the region in general rather than this tea. Today it is listed among Sichuan's better-known greens and has collected a string of provincial and national brand titles.
